scope: Exact-island lower bound from the locally supported, resource-pressured Guanche population of Tenerife at the end of the pre-Hispanic period

promotion_audit.decision: Tenerife is an exact bounded island and maps one-to-one to the EU5 aguere location. A peer-reviewed archaeological and palaeodemographic study reconstructs 15,000-20,000 Guanche inhabitants at conquest, documents the island's complete territorial allocation, and independently links northern agricultural intensification, physiological stress and mortality to population pressure. Pre-Hispanic subsistence was locally produced and late-period isolation prevents a far-away staple-import explanation. Because conquest and the 1494-1495 epidemic affect the endpoint and no formal saturation fraction is published, only the conservative 15,000-person lower edge is used for training.

records.label: Pre-Hispanic Tenerife / Guanche island population at conquest
records.interval_semantics: Rodriguez-Martin et al. (2000), Tables and conclusions, reconstruct approximately 15,500 inhabitants from archaeological sites dated around the 1496 conquest and conclude that the defensible island total is 15,000-20,000. The study also records 1,380 km2 divided among nine menceyatos plus 654 km2 of communal mid/high-mountain pasture, together accounting for Tenerife's full 2,034 km2. The 15,000 lower edge is used unchanged as a one-sided capacity floor. The local-food interval reflects an internally differentiated but island-based diet; marine food was under 5%, and agriculture, gathering, herding, meat and dairy were all local. It does not claim that the 15,000-20,000 population interval is itself a carrying-capacity interval.
pressure_evidence: Rodriguez-Martin et al. (2000), population table and pp. 118-119: archaeological sites near conquest yield about 15,500 inhabitants distributed across all nine menceyatos; the conclusion gives a 15,000-20,000 island interval.

Rodriguez-Martin et al. (2000), pp. 121-130: northern Tenerife had roughly double the southern density; agriculture and plant gathering intensified there, and the authors explicitly infer that differentiated resource exploitation was driven by northern population pressure.

Rodriguez-Martin et al. (2000), pp. 95, 123-130: Tacoronte obtained about three quarters of diet from plant resources, northern children aged 6-10 show 50% more Harris lines, and the authors connect greater plant dependence to metabolic/physiological stress, morbidity and higher mortality.

Rodriguez-Martin et al. (2000), pp. 124-128: local dry farming produced wheat, barley and broad beans, smaller-scale irrigation existed, southern subsistence emphasized goat/sheep herding, meat and dairy, and chemical/dental evidence independently reconstructs the north-south dietary contrast; marine resources were below 5%.

Rodriguez-Martin et al. (2000), pp. 135-143: the authors reject a 35,000-person estimate because Tenerife lacked capacity to support it and describe the most isolated Anaga mountain population as near extinction, supporting a resource-constrained rather than import-supported island system.

Atoche-Pena and del-Arco-Aguilar (European Journal of Archaeology, 2024), section on demographic stress and carrying capacity: intensive Canarian settlement is associated with demographic stress, surplus storage, crop diversification and mixed subsistence; palaeogenetics indicates an isolation phase from the ninth through fourteenth centuries.
records.trade_dependence: Very low for staple calories. The pre-Hispanic island economy described by bioarchaeology used Tenerife-grown cereals and pulses, local gathered plants, local goats/sheep and dairy, with a small local marine share. Archaeometric synthesis indicates long isolation before European conquest. The 0.97 lower edge allows minor exchange/contact without treating it as material food import dependence.
records.boundary_description: The entire island of Tenerife, 2,034 km2 in the cited palaeodemographic study, partitioned into nine menceyatos occupying about 1,380 km2 and about 654 km2 of communal middle/high-mountain pasture.
records.boundary_source: Rodriguez-Martin et al. (2000), island and menceyato area table; exact modern Tenerife coastline
records.source_family_independence: The population reconstruction, skeletal mortality and dietary-stress evidence belong to the Tenerife Guanche bioarchaeological literature and are treated as one source family. The 2024 archaeometric synthesis is used for independent review of isolation and carrying-capacity adaptations, not as a separate anchor.
records.notes: This is an unusually strong lower-bound case because boundary, locally supported diet and independent pressure evidence all align. It remains one-sided: the 1494-1495 epidemic, conquest disruption and absence of a literature-supported saturation fraction prevent using the 15,000-20,000 population interval as a two-sided Malthusian capacity target. Technology is accepted as comparable to 1337 because the observation remains within the fixed 1100-1500 window and describes the indigenous pre-conquest food system, not colonial agriculture.
